av_event.line_text: Rowena: It is, yeah. My mum and dad are still in Batangas. I video call, I send money, but it's not the same as being there. Sorry, that got heavy!
av_event.what: Rowena's voice catches slightly on 'being there'. She pauses for about a second, looks down and away from the camera, and blinks a few times behind her glasses before she smiles again and carries on.

text:
A: Hiya! Hello, can you hear me?
B: Yes, hello! I'm Agnieszka. You can say Aga, it's easier.
A: Aga! I'm Rowena. Oh, I was hoping I'd get you. I saw your shift rota on the fridge in the photo and thought, she's one of us.
B: [laughs] Yes! Senior care assistant, care home in Yeovil. Forty-eight beds. And you?
A: Nurse. Tissue viability, at the hospital in Warrington. So pressure ulcers, wounds.
B: Oh, so you are the person we call when somebody's heels are red and we panic!
A: That's me! Honestly, care homes are where it starts or stops, you know. If the carers are turning people properly and checking the skin, I've got nothing to do. You're the ones catching it.
B: Thank you. People don't say that much. Usually it's "why is this paperwork not done." And we are short-staffed again, three long days, I'm knackered.
A: Oh, three long days. You poor thing. Do you get a day off now?
B: Tomorrow, yes. I walk the dog, Biscuit, he's Mark's, my husband's, old cocker spaniel. But if it's raining he just sits at the door and looks at me like I'm crazy.
A: [laughs] Clever dog. Where are you from originally? I'm guessing not Yeovil.
B: Rzeszów, in Poland. South-east. I came at twenty-two, so, eighteen years.
A: Snap, almost! Philippines, Batangas. 2003. I shared a house with five other nurses when I first came, I cried every night for about six months.
B: Oh, I know this feeling. First job was hotel kitchen in Somerset, I didn't know anybody. And now my mum is getting older and I'm here looking after other people's mums. It's strange, no?
A: It is, yeah. My mum and dad are still in Batangas. I video call, I send money, but it's not the same as being there. Sorry, that got heavy!
B: No, it's okay. I think everyone like us feels it. I go to Mass and I light a candle, it helps a bit.
A: Me too. I sing in the Filipino choir at my parish. We've got a fiesta coming up, so it's practice every Thursday.
B: Thursday is my Zumba! With two girls from work. It's more laughing than dancing.
A: I do Zumba on Tuesdays! Our instructor plays the same five songs every week. I could do it in my sleep.
B: [laughs] Ours too! Always "Despacito." Every week, "Despacito."
A: Oh, it's the law, I think. Do you cook Polish food at home?
B: All the time. Pierogi in big batches for the freezer. Mark says I made him half-Polish with food only.
A: [laughs] My brother-in-law's the same with adobo. He's from Warrington, he'd never had rice with everything before me.
B: And now?
A: Now he asks where the rice is! We should swap recipes, Aga. Pierogi for lumpia.
B: Yes, deal! But you have to tell me which is the best Zumba song.
A: None of them. That's the answer.
